---
title: "Wind speed"
subtitle: "Characterization of the cadcat 10 m wind speed"
date: last-modified
---

**Purpose.** Characterize Cal-Adapt Analytics Engine 10 m wind speed
(`wspeed` / `wspd10mean`), 1980–2014, against the quality dimensions fixed in
[Scope & Definitions](../method/scope-and-definitions.qmd). Findings derived here
feed the [good/bad matrix](../guidance/good-bad-matrix.qmd).

Evaluated against **station observations** from
[HDP](https://github.com/Eagle-Rock-Analytics/historical-obs-platform) first, then
against [CONUS404](https://www.usgs.gov/data/conus404-four-kilometer-long-term-regional-hydroclimate-reanalysis-over-conterminous-united)
and [ERA5](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/reanalysis-era5-single-levels?tab=overview).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Headline

**The products are right where we can check them, and can be wrong in a way the mean
does not show.**

At flat, open airport stations, the exposure class closest to what a grid cell
represents, both products are unbiased: LOCA2 **0.996**, WRF **0.995** across
207 stations.

But the *distribution* is too narrow. Observed Weibull shape `k` is **1.51**; the
products give **2.18** and **2.92**. At those same stations both **under-predict
wind power density by 13–19 %**, and produce days above 10 m/s at **2.7 % against
an observed 10.5 %**, one quarter of the observed rate.

:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Compare against observations first

The first obvious way that comes to mind when reviewing a gridded product is to compare it against a
reanalysis. The ratio between AE's WRF/LOCA2 and ERA5 is **1.5–1.6 over land**,
which reads as a 60 % error, and is not one.

**ERA5 at 0.25° (~31 km) cannot represent a 3 km ridge–valley contrast**, so over
terrain the two are measuring different things and neither is wrong for
disagreeing. §7 uses ERA5 as a common grid and a diagnostic, not as truth.
:::

---

## 1. What the stations can and cannot be

Stations are the **primary reference**, not a common frame in the gridding sense,
and the difference matters:

- **They are points.** A station samples one spot; a LOCA2/WRF cell averages
  9 km² and an ERA5 cell ~950 km². Part of every model–station difference is this
  footprint mismatch and cannot be removed.
- **They do not cover the ocean**, and they are sparse above 2,000 m, exactly
  where §7 shows the products and ERA5 diverge most.

So a gridded comparison still earns its place, for spatial and seasonal structure
and for the ocean control. That is what §7 uses ERA5 for.

### Screening

**338 of 1,207 stations were removed**, and the breakdown matters for how the
archive is described:

| reason | n |
|---|---|
| record < 60 months | 292 |
| < 20 distinct values (stuck sensor) | 98 |
| observed mean < 0.5 m/s | 46 |
| excluded prefix `RAWS_TR` | 73 |

**869 stations retained.**

### The observed distribution is not remotely Gaussian

Pooled over **108 million valid hourly observations**: mean 2.47 m/s, median
2.00, p90 5.37, p99 10.20.

::: {#fig-dist-hourly .column-page-inset}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="dist_stations_hourly">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/dist_stations_hourly.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Observed hourly wind speed, pooled across the analysis stations. The zero spike and the mass below 1.5 m/s are reporting convention as much as wind.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**13.2 % of values are exactly zero** and **38.3 % fall below 1.5 m/s**. The zero
spike is the ASOS calm floor, reports below roughly 3 kt are recorded as 0 and
No model can reproduce it. **Every model/observation ratio in this page is
therefore slightly generous to the model.**
:::

::: {#fig-dist-monthly .column-page-inset}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="dist_stations_monthly">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/dist_stations_monthly.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
The same observations aggregated to monthly means — the cadence at which products and observations are most often compared. The calm floor and the broad tail both disappear, which is why a monthly comparison cannot see the failure in §5.
:::

## 2. Level at station locations {#sec-level}

**At airports, agreement between both products and observations is remarkable:**
Median `model / observation` of **0.996 (LOCA2)** and **0.995 (WRF)** across 207
flat, open stations. Two entirely different downscaling methods land within half
a percent of observations and of each other.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Unbiased is not accurate:** Only **33 % of airport stations** fall within ±10 %
for WRF (**48 %** for LOCA2); the IQRs are 0.84–1.15 and 0.88–1.10. The errors
cancel across 200 stations rather than being individually small, the signature of
point-versus-area sampling. For a user siting a single project, the ±10 % figure
is very relevant.
:::

**Every other station class reads low relative to the products.**

| class | n | observed mean | LOCA2 | WRF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| airport | 207 | **2.90 m/s** | 0.996 | 0.995 |
| vegetated (RAWS) | 469 | 2.41 m/s | 1.171 | 1.517 |
| irrigated (CIMIS) | 173 | 1.96 m/s | 1.403 | 1.488 |

**Airports record more wind than any other class despite sitting lowest:**
median 135 m against RAWS's 1,094 m. RAWS masts are often on ridges but exist to
represent wildland fire danger, fuel moisture and ecological conditions, so they
sit in vegetation-representative clearings; canopy shelter dominates.

**LOCA2 and WRF diverge sharply at sheltered sites:** 1.17 against 1.52 at RAWS,
while being identical at airports. LOCA2 is smoother over complex terrain,
produces less terrain-driven acceleration, and so lands nearer observations that
are themselves sheltered.


::: {#fig-agreement-maps}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="station_agreement_maps">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/station_agreement_maps.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Per-station model/observation ratio. Scatter within a region is as large as the difference between regions.  The siting effect made visible, and it is why only the airport class can grade the products.
:::

### 2.1 Does a product explain the variation *between* sites?

**Both products explain between-site variation far better than ERA5.**

| network | ERA5 | LOCA2 | WRF |
|---|---|---|---|
| ASOSAWOS | 0.321 | 0.668 | **0.681** |
| OtherISD | 0.391 | **0.670** | 0.518 |
| CIMIS | 0.065 | 0.571 | **0.656** |
| RAWS | 0.294 | **0.799** | 0.444 |

**ERA5's `std_ratio` of 0.495 is the resolution deficit made visible at points.**
A 31 km field carries only half the station-to-station variance that exists; both
km-scale-informed products recover most of it (0.86 and 0.92). The km-scale
products carry real point-scale information that ERA5 does not.

---

## 3. Between products, at station locations {#sec-between}

::: {#fig-between}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="between_products_stations">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/between_products_stations.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Product against product at each station, with observations. The spread perpendicular to the 1:1 line is what neither product resolves. 
:::

**The two WRF drivers are interchangeable**, which is what licenses treating them
as one product: median difference **+0.60 %**, IQR **−0.76 % to +1.65 %**. The
driver changes the weather, not the climate.

**The products differ depending on where they are measured:**

| | all stations | airport | irrigated |
|---|---|---|---|
| LOCA2 | 1.166 | **0.996** | 1.403 |
| WRF | 1.354 | **0.995** | 1.488 |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The pooled column is the least useful number in the table.** LOCA2 1.166
against WRF 1.354 looks like a substantive difference between products, but it is
largely a difference in how each responds to stations sheltered by amounts
neither model knows. §4 asks the same question without that confusion.
:::

---

## 4. CONUS404: do independent km-scale models agree? {#sec-conus404}

On CONUS404's own 4 km grid, with no coarse field involved:

| product | median ratio | n_cells |
|---|---|---|
| **WRF** | **1.020** | 225,848 |
| LOCA2 | **0.902** | 49,773 |

**Two independently built km-scale models agree to 2 %.** Different institutions,
different configurations, different land-surface and physics choices.

**LOCA2 at 0.902 sits 10 % below an independent km-scale model** while sitting
29 % *above* ERA5 (§7). Statistical downscaling inherits the smoother field it was
trained to reproduce and does not manufacture the acceleration a dynamical model
generates.

**Taken with §2 the picture is consistent.** At airports both products are right.
Away from airports LOCA2 is lower than WRF; against an unobstructed km-scale
comparator LOCA2 is lower than WRF.

---

## 5. Distribution shape and extremes {#sec-extremes}

**This is where both products have issues with respect to the observations, and monthly means hide it completely.**

::: {#fig-dist-daily}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="dist_daily_stations">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/dist_daily_stations.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Daily wind speed at all analysis stations. Left: density, the products peak too high and too narrow. Centre: log density, where the tail deficit shows. Right: Q–Q against observations.
:::

::: {#fig-dist-airports}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="dist_daily_airports">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/dist_daily_airports.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
The same at airport stations only, where the mean is right to within half a percent. The shape failure is independent of the level agreement.
:::

**Weibull `k` describes the balance between calm and windy days**; lower `k`
means a broader distribution.

| source | mean | k (shape) | A (scale) | power W/m² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **stations** | 2.43 | **1.51** | 2.69 | 23.7 |
| LOCA2 | 2.94 | 2.18 | 3.32 | 27.4 |
| WRF | 3.40 | **2.92** | 3.81 | 34.3 |
| ERA5 | 2.16 | 2.32 | 2.44 | 10.3 |

Observed `k` is **1.51**; the products give **2.18 and 2.92**, too few calm days
*and* too few windy ones.

**At airports, where the level is right, both under-predict power density:**

| source | speed ratio | power ratio |
|---|---|---|
| LOCA2 | 0.977 | **0.812** |
| WRF | 1.077 | **0.875** |
| ERA5 | 0.757 | 0.355 |

A product matching observed mean wind to within 8 % delivers **13–19 % less power
density**, the number a resource assessment or calculation will inherit.

### Upper tail

::: {#fig-extremes .column-page-inset}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="extremes_stations">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/extremes_stations.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Daily maxima, observed against modelled. Quantile ratios fall monotonically toward q99, so the distribution is too narrow at the top rather than merely displaced.
:::

| group | mean ratio | q90 ratio | q99 ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| all stations | 1.124 | 0.974 | **0.867** |
| airports | 0.835 | 0.786 | **0.782** |

**The ratios fall monotonically with quantile.** A scale-factor error would keep
them flat. Falling ratios mean the modelled distribution is too narrow at the
top, agreeing with the Weibull shape above, arrived at independently from daily
maxima.

## 6. Seasonal and regional structure {#sec-seasonal}

::: {#fig-seasonal .column-page-inset}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="seasonal_stations">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/seasonal_stations.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Seasonal cycle of agreement at station locations. Nearly flat, with a mild winter excess.
:::

- The seasonal cycle of agreement is resolved comparably across regions.
- **Both products agree slightly better in summer than in winter.**
- **LOCA2 peaks in January almost everywhere** (6 of 8 regions) while WRF's peak
  month scatters across October, November, December, January and May, a
  statistical method inheriting one domain-wide seasonal signature, and a
  dynamical model producing region-specific seasonality.

### 6.1 Regional structure

::: {#fig-regions}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="region_assignment">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/region_assignment.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Region assignment from station coordinates and elevation. Worth checking before reading the table below — the boxes are approximate and go wrong at edges.
:::

::: {#fig-agreement-region}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="agreement_by_region">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/agreement_by_region.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Agreement by California climate region: median, spread, and the airport-only subset. The airport column is the unconfounded one.
:::

**Agreement is regionally uniform at airports and regionally structured
everywhere else.**

| region | n_air | LOCA2 | WRF |
|---|---|---|---|
| North Coast | 12 | 1.122 | 1.050 |
| Bay & Delta | 25 | 1.046 | **0.811** |
| Central Coast | 8 | 0.983 | 0.917 |
| South Coast | 60 | 1.052 | 0.952 |
| Sierra Nevada | 11 | 1.018 | 1.106 |
| Central Valley | 25 | 0.996 | 1.064 |
| Mojave/Sonoran | 46 | **0.873** | 1.020 |
| Northeast | 10 | **0.827** | 1.110 |

**Most regions sit within ±10 % of 1.0 for both products.** The domain-wide
airport result of §2 is not an average of large opposing regional errors; it holds
region by region.

**The exceptions are informative and not shared.** LOCA2 runs low in the Mojave
(0.873) and Northeast (0.827). The two most arid, thermally driven regions, 
where WRF is fine (1.020, 1.110). WRF runs low in the Bay & Delta (0.811), the one
region whose wind climate is dominated by a sea breeze through a single
topographic feature. **Each product fails in a regime the other handles.**

---

## 7. ERA5: where and when coarse and fine fields diverge {#sec-era5}

Used as a common grid and a diagnostic, not as truth, and for the one thing it
is uniquely good for: complete uniform coverage, which supplies a **control
region** where the mechanism under test should switch off.

::: {#fig-ratio-region .column-page-inset}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-frame" data-fig="ratio_by_region">
  <iframe src="../figures/html/ratio_by_region.html" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```
Ratio against ERA5 by region and terrain. WRF's response rises with sub-grid relief; LOCA2's stays flat, the signature of a statistically downscaled field inheriting a smoother target.
:::

**Over open water the km-scale models and ERA5 agree to within half a percent.
Over land they diverge by 52–62 %.**

| product | ocean | coastal | land | pooled |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WRF | **0.995** | 1.167 | **1.617** | 1.458 |
| CONUS404 | **0.996** | 1.180 | **1.522** | 1.124 |
| LOCA2 | — | 1.163 | 1.289 | 1.285 |

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The ocean column is a positive control and it is decisive.** WRF 0.995 and
CONUS404 0.996. Two independently configured 3–4 km models agreeing with a 31 km
reanalysis to within 0.5 % where there is no sub-grid terrain to resolve.

A calibration error would
bias a model *everywhere*, including over water. It does not. **So the land
disagreement is a resolution difference, not an error.**
:::

---

## 8. What this means for the matrix

| dimension | LOCA2 | WRF |
|---|---|---|
| mean bias | ✅ 0.996 at airports | ✅ 0.995 at airports |
| spatial pattern | ⚠️ too smooth (0.902 vs CONUS404) | ✅ 1.020 vs CONUS404 |
| terrain response | ⚠️ flat across elevation bands | ✅ tracks sub-grid relief |
| seasonal structure | ✅ flat ratio, one domain-wide peak | ✅ flat ratio, regional peaks |
| diurnal structure | ❓ no hourly data | ❓ — hourly analysis not done |
| extremes | ❓ no max-wind variable | ⚠️ tail 13 % short at q99 |
| distribution shape | ⚠️ k = 2.18 vs 1.51 | ⚠️ k = 2.92 vs 1.51 |

**The pattern across the row is the finding.** Both products pass on level and
fail on shape. The use cases users actually bring would determine whether this limitation is critical.

---

## 9. Caveats

### On the observational reference

1. **Only airports are unobstructed.** Every other class confounds model error
   with shelter (§2)..
2. **Footprint.** A station is a point; a LOCA2 cell averages 9 km² and an ERA5
   cell ~950 km². Part of §2's "only a third within ±10 %" is this and cannot be
   removed.
3. **A calm floor.** 13.2 % of hourly observations are exactly zero, the ASOS/AWOS
   sub-3-kt convention. No model reproduces it, so observed means are biased low
   and **every ratio here is slightly generous to the model**.
4. **Reporting quantisation.** Harmless for means; relevant to §5's Weibull fits
   and quantile ratios.
5. **338 of 1,207 stations screened out**, 292 for records under 60 months. The
   retained 869 are not a random sample of the archive.
6. **Coverage gaps.** No ocean stations, and few unobstructed high-terrain
   stations, the Sierra has 11 airports against 73 RAWS. The products are least
   verifiable exactly where §7 shows they diverge most from ERA5.

### On what is not measured

11. **No uncertainty.** Every result is a median with no bootstrap, no confidence
    interval, no effective sample size for autocorrelated series.
12. **No hourly data in this analysis**, so no diurnal analysis. It is not
    settled how valid a model-against-hourly-station comparison would be.
13. **Historical only.** No check that skill is stationary under warming.
